sceneEn: You are talking to a sleep consultant: your habits before bed, what happens in the night, how you wake in the morning. Describe the order with bevor and während.
partnerEn: a sleep consultant who asks about the daily routine step by step
openingEn: Please describe your evening to me: what do you do in the two hours before you go to bed?
goalEn: Your habits before bed, what happens in the night and how you wake in the morning have all been described.

sceneEn: You are telling a friend you trust that you have been struggling lately: what is weighing on you, when it started, what helps. Build it with fixed-preposition verbs.
partnerEn: a friend who knows how to listen and does not rush you
openingEn: You've seemed different for a few weeks. Do you want to tell me what's going on?
goalEn: What is weighing on you and when it started have been described, and what helps has been discussed.

sceneEn: You are telling the nurse at the emergency department what happened: what happened, in what order, and where it hurts now. Order it by pulling the earlier event back.
partnerEn: an emergency nurse who asks quick, clear questions
openingEn: Just stay sitting quietly. Tell me briefly: what happened and when was that?
goalEn: What happened has been told in order and where it hurts now has been said.

sceneEn: You are at your vaccination appointment: ask what you need to bring, about the possible side effects and when the booster is due. Repeat the passive sentences you hear in your own words.
partnerEn: a practice worker who speaks briefly and clearly
openingEn: Good afternoon. Have you got your vaccination card with you? Then we'll see what's being done today.
goalEn: What you need to bring, the possible side effects and the timing of the booster have all been found out.

sceneEn: You are visiting a relative in hospital: ask how they are, offer help, cheer them up. Soften your offers with the subjunctive.
partnerEn: a relative who is tired but wants to talk
openingEn: How lovely that you're here. Sit down — and tell me something from outside, will you?
goalEn: How they are has been asked, help has been offered and their spirits have been lifted.

sceneEn: You are asking a neighbour about the rubbish rules in the building you have just moved into: which rubbish goes in which bin, how the deposit is claimed back, which day it is collected.
partnerEn: a slightly meticulous neighbour who knows the rules well
openingEn: You're new here, aren't you? Everyone gets the rubbish wrong at first — what would you like to know?
goalEn: Which rubbish goes where and how the deposit is claimed back have both been found out.

sceneEn: You are discussing the rising electricity bill with your flatmate: what you suggest changing and why. Give the aim of your suggestions with um … zu.
partnerEn: a flatmate who likes their comfort and is wary of saving
openingEn: The electricity bill has got really high. But I don't want to sit in the dark — what do you suggest?
goalEn: At least two suggestions have been made along with their aim, and one has been agreed on.

sceneEn: You are arguing with a colleague about how to get to work: by car, by bike or by public transport. Set both sides out with paired conjunctions and justify your own choice.
partnerEn: a practical colleague who is attached to their car
openingEn: You cycle every day now? In this weather? Well, I'm sticking with the car — go on, convince me.
goalEn: The pros and cons of both sides have been given and your own choice has been defended with reasons.

sceneEn: You and a friend are talking about your shopping habits: which products you go for, which shops you go to, why. Describe your choices with relative clauses.
partnerEn: a friend who watches the price but is open to persuasion
openingEn: You only shop at the packaging-free shop now? Isn't that much more expensive? Do tell.
goalEn: Which products and shops you go for has been described along with your reasons.

sceneEn: You are explaining the rules to someone who wants to join the community garden: when the work happens, how the harvest is shared, who is responsible for what. Give the rules in passive sentences.
partnerEn: an eager new member who knows nothing at all
openingEn: I'd love to join in. How does it actually work here — do you have to come every week?
goalEn: The work day, the sharing of the harvest and the responsibilities have been described, and the new member has said what they have decided.

sceneEn: You are talking to a neighbour about how the weather has changed: how it used to be, how it is now, what you notice. Describe the change with comparative forms.
partnerEn: a long-standing neighbour who likes comparing the years
openingEn: We never used to have a summer like this. Do you notice it too, or am I imagining it?
goalEn: Then and now have been compared and what you have noticed has been described.

sceneEn: You are at an introductory meeting at a voluntary organisation: say why you want to volunteer, how much time you have a week and what you could do.
partnerEn: a warm but realistic volunteer coordinator
openingEn: Glad you could come. First tell me: why do you want to get involved with us?
goalEn: Your reason for volunteering, the time you can give and what you could do have all been described.

sceneEn: You are talking about the changes with someone who has lived in the area a long time: what has been done up, what has closed, what has happened to the rents, who has left. Describe the change in the past passive.
partnerEn: a resident who resents the change and misses the old area
openingEn: You should have seen this neighbourhood ten years ago. Do you know what's disappeared from here?
goalEn: What has been done up, what has closed and what has happened to the rents have all been discussed.

sceneEn: A journalist is talking to you at a demonstration: why you are here, what you are demanding, what you want changed. Give your aim in damit clauses.
partnerEn: a local journalist who wants short, clear answers
openingEn: Excuse me, briefly for our paper: why are you here today?
goalEn: Why you are there and what you are demanding have been said, and what you want changed has been described.

sceneEn: You are talking to a worker at the animal shelter: which animal you could look after, what sort of home is needed, what the daily responsibility is. Describe the animals with relative clauses.
partnerEn: an honest shelter worker who knows the animals very well
openingEn: Come with me, I'll show you the animals. Are you looking for an animal for yourself or for the family?
goalEn: Which animal you could look after, what sort of home is needed and the daily responsibility have all been discussed.

sceneEn: You and a friend are playing a 'what if' game: what you would do if you were rich, where you would live, what you would not change. Build your answers with unreal conditional clauses.
partnerEn: a friend who loves daydreaming and keeps producing questions
openingEn: Imagine you win a million tomorrow. What would you do first?
goalEn: What you would do if you were rich, where you would live and what you would not change have all been said.

sceneEn: You and a friend are sharing your wishes: what you would ask for if you had three wishes, which wish has still not come true. Build your answers in the subjunctive.
partnerEn: a warm friend who tells you their own wishes too
openingEn: If you had three wishes free — but honestly, no millions: what would your three be?
goalEn: Three wishes have been given and it has been said which one has still not come true.

sceneEn: You are telling a friend about a decision you made in the past: what had happened, what you should have done looking back, whether you regret it now. Use the patterns of regret.
partnerEn: a friend who does not judge and tells you their own regrets
openingEn: You said the other day you still think about that business a lot. What would you have done differently?
goalEn: The decision has been described, what you should have done looking back has been said and how you see it today has been given.

sceneEn: You are talking to someone close about your fears for the future: what you are afraid will go wrong, what you would do in the worst case, what reassures you.
partnerEn: someone close who calms you down and makes you think with questions
openingEn: You've seemed on edge since the decision came up. What's the worst possibility you're thinking of?
goalEn: The fear has been named, what you would do in the worst case has been said and what reassures you has been discussed.

sceneEn: You have run into an old friend after years: what has happened in between, why the friendship lapsed, how things are now. Order it by pulling the earlier event back.
partnerEn: a talkative old friend who is sorry to have lost touch
openingEn: I don't believe it — how long has it been? Tell me, what's been happening with you?
goalEn: What happened in between has been described, the reason for the lapse has been discussed and you have promised to meet again.

sceneEn: You are telling someone you have been friends with for a long time how you feel: what you feel, what you are suggesting, and that you want to keep the friendship whatever the answer. Soften your sentences with the subjunctive.
partnerEn: a surprised but warm friend who asks for time to think
openingEn: You wanted to talk about something and you look so serious. Now I'm curious — what is it?
goalEn: Your feeling has been said, an offer has been made and it has been made clear that the friendship will go on whatever the answer.

sceneEn: You are talking through a problem between you and someone close: what happened, how you felt, what you want to happen. Instead of blame, give your aim in damit clauses.
partnerEn: someone close who is defensive at first but opens up to listening
openingEn: You've been odd with me for days. Will you please tell me what's actually going on?
goalEn: What happened and how you felt have been described without blame, and what you want to happen has been said.

sceneEn: Someone is asking you about your life between two countries: what it was like when you arrived, what you miss, where you feel you belong now. Tell the past moments with als.
partnerEn: an unhurried acquaintance who is genuinely interested
openingEn: May I ask you something personal? Where do you actually feel at home — here or there?
goalEn: How your arrival was, what you miss and where you feel you belong now have all been described.

sceneEn: You are telling someone about your big dream: what it is, why you want it, what the first step would be and what is holding you back. Build the dream with infinitive phrases.
partnerEn: a supportive listener who asks realistic questions
openingEn: You once told me about a plan you'd had in mind for years. What became of it?
goalEn: Your dream, your reason, the first step and what is holding you back have all been described.

sceneEn: You are having a mid-course review with your teacher: how the road has gone, what was hardest, what you are proud of, what you will do next.
partnerEn: a proud teacher who has followed you from the start
openingEn: We're at the end of the first part. Look back a moment: what was the most important moment for you?
goalEn: How the road has gone, the hardest part, what you are proud of and your next goal have all been described.
